title: The Postcards of Milton Flats
premise: Mirabel Vasquez has spent a decade writing postcards to their grandmother's burned-down house in Milton Flats, letters no one will ever answer, until a radio song turns out to be one their grandmother composed and never recorded — performed by the man who may have stolen it. Following the song's trail, Mirabel uncovers the family secret everyone arranged themselves around: that grandmother's brother, not an accident, set the fire to bury what she knew about his theft. The last bus route to the old neighborhood is being permanently rerouted, forcing Mirabel to return, confront the uncle now dying in a care home, and choose between legal restitution and a quieter justice — publicly crediting the song at its first proper recording. In the end, Mirabel mails one final postcard, addressed to no address at all, and lets the family inherit the truth instead of the silence.
about_author: Mirabel Iversen is a former archivist who spent years cataloguing unclaimed correspondence in municipal storage, an experience that haunts everything they write. They live near a decommissioned rail line and insist their novels begin as overheard melodies.

chapters.title: The Smile That Ends Conversations
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. We meet them at the post office counter, mailing postcards to an address that burned down in 2011, deflecting a clerk's friendly questions with practiced ease. A coworker's wedding invitation forces Mirabel to confront how thoroughly they've arranged their life around avoidance. Emotional beat: loneliness disguised as self-sufficiency.

chapters.title: Postcards to Ash
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV, flashback braided with present. We learn the ritual: every Sunday, a postcard to Grandma Rosa at 44 Delmore Street, describing weather, small victories, nothing true. The fire report — 'cause undetermined' — sits in a shoebox. Beat: grief maintained on purpose, because answers would end something.

chapters.title: A Song Out of Turn
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. Driving home, a late-night radio program plays an unfamiliar tune — and it is Rosa's song, the one she hummed while cooking, the one she said was 'not finished yet.' The DJ credits a composer named Edwin Vasquez. Mirabel pulls over, shaking. Beat: the past reaching through the static.

chapters.title: Uncle Edwin's Long Career
chapters.summary: Mirabel researches Edwin Vasquez: minor regional fame, three albums, a career built quietly in the next county. Cousin Dani warns them off by phone: 'You don't want to know what we all agreed not to know.' Beat: the family's architecture of silence becomes visible.

chapters.title: What the Fire Report Didn't Say
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. At the records office, an aging clerk remembers the Delmore Street fire and mentions an insurance dispute that vanished when Edwin paid everyone off. First hint that money bought more than silence — it bought a version of events. Beat: suspicion hardening into purpose.

chapters.title: The Rerouting Notice
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. The transit authority announces the 47 bus line — the only route into old Milton Flats — will be permanently rerouted in six weeks for redevelopment. The neighborhood itself is being erased on schedule. Beat: external deadline fuses with internal one; the door is literally closing.

chapters.title: Dani at the Diner
chapters.summary: Alternating POV begins: cousin Dani, a hospice nurse, narrates her side. She meets Mirabel at a diner and reveals fragments: Rosa and Edwin fought over a notebook of songs; Rosa claimed half of everything; weeks later, the fire. Dani signed a statement she didn't believe. Beat: complicity inherited like eye color.

chapters.title: Forty-Four Delmore Street
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. Riding the 47 one last time before rerouting, Mirabel walks the block where the house stood — now a chain-link lot slated for condos. They find a melted hinge in the weeds and pocket it like a relic. Beat: mourning a place that was already a fiction.

chapters.title: The Care Home on Kessler Avenue
chapters.summary: Edwin's POV, first time. Dying of heart failure, Edwin hears from a nurse that someone has been asking about Delmore Street. He begins dictating a letter he never sends. His chapter reveals charm as a lifelong instrument. Beat: the antagonist made human without being absolved.

chapters.title: The Notebook Problem
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. Dani produces a photograph: Rosa's songbook, spiral-bound, seen once at a family gathering in 2010 — then never again. If it survived the fire, someone took it out first. Beat: the object of inheritance identified; proof requires possession.

chapters.title: Conversations With a Thief
chapters.summary: Mirabel visits Edwin under a false pretext — a 'local music history project.' He performs warmth beautifully, tells stories, denies nothing directly. When Mirabel hums four bars of Rosa's song, his face does something complicated. Beat: a duel conducted entirely in manners.

chapters.title: Rosa's Half
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV, deep flashback reconstructed from letters. Rosa's voice emerges: her songs, her plans to record, her fury at a brother who 'borrowed' her future and called it family loyalty. Beat: the grandmother becomes a full person, not a wound.

chapters.title: The Statement Dani Signed
chapters.summary: Dani's POV. She recounts the aftermath of the fire: adults coaching children, a lawyer's language, the family closing ranks around Edwin because he paid for Grandpa's surgery. Her guilt has calcified into caretaking him. Beat: justice deferred becomes justice denied.

chapters.title: Lawyers, Briefly
chapters.summary: Mirabel consults a pro bono attorney: no notebook, no witnesses willing to testify, statute limitations on the arson, copyright murky after decades. The law offers almost nothing. 'What do you actually want?' the lawyer asks. Mirabel can't answer yet. Beat: the theme named — justice outside the law.

chapters.title: The Radio Man Remembers
chapters.summary: Mirabel tracks down the DJ, Gus, who received Edwin's demo tape anonymously in 2012 — postmarked the week after the fire. Someone mailed Edwin the evidence of his own theft, or Edwin mailed himself an alibi. Either way, the tape exists. Beat: the plot's mechanism clicks into view.

chapters.title: Breaking the Arrangement
chapters.summary: Family meeting POV, rotating among cousins. Mirabel lays out everything at a Sunday dinner. The room splits: some want peace, some want money, Aunt Lorraine screams that Rosa would have wanted family kept whole. Beat: climax of the social plot — the arrangement shatters.

chapters.title: What Edwin Kept
chapters.summary: Edwin's POV. Alone, he opens a cedar chest: Rosa's notebook, kept twenty years, read a thousand times, never used beyond those few stolen songs. He knows exactly what he is. He writes Rosa's name inside the cover for the first time. Beat: confession without audience.

chapters.title: The Last Bus
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. Final day of the 47 route. Mirabel rides it end to end with the melted hinge in their pocket, deciding between lawsuit, exposure, or something stranger. Dani sits down beside them uninvited. Beat: stillness before the choice.

chapters.title: Kessler Avenue, Night
chapters.summary: Mirabel and Dani confront Edwin together. No cameras, no lawyers. They play him Rosa's song from a phone recording of the radio broadcast. He gives them the notebook — not as surrender but as 'returning borrowed property.' Beat: climax; justice negotiated face to face.

chapters.title: Credit Where Due
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. Through Gus and a small label, they arrange the song's first legitimate recording — co-credited to Rosa Vasquez, proceeds endowed to the Milton Flats tenants' fund fighting the redevelopment. Not a courtroom victory; a public correction. Beat: justice as restoration, not punishment.

chapters.title: The Arrangement, Rearranged
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs. The family absorbs the truth unevenly — some estranged, some relieved, Dani finally sleeping well. Edwin dies in early spring; at the funeral, half the family sings Rosa's song, and it doesn't resolve the way anyone expects. Beat: inheritance redefined as story, not property.

chapters.title: One More Postcard
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. At the post office, they mail a final postcard — blank except for 'It's finished now' — addressed simply to 'Rosa.' Then they turn down the clerk's invitation to coffee... and reconsider. The smile softens into something real. Beat: identity rebuilt; the letter-writer finally open to reply.
